lines.text: In eighteen fifty-eight, a suffocating smell rose across central London.
Hot summer weather exacerbated the stench of untreated human waste along the River Thames.
For years, an inadequate sewer system had emptied directly into the waterway.
People believed that miasma from the effluent transmitted contagious diseases.
Three outbreaks of cholera had already been blamed on the ongoing river problems.
The crisis finally forced parliament to accept a proposal from civil engineer Joseph Bazalgette.
He designed a vast network of intercepting sewers to move effluent eastward.
Massive pumping stations were built to lift the sewage into new outfall pipes.
This monumental engineering achievement ultimately cleansed the river.
